evals.prompt: My CompileIQ search on a layernorm kernel finished (single objective, minimizing latency in ms) and dumped its results to /workspace/input/results_layernorm.csv. Pull out the top 5 configs for me. The best one is about 8% below my 1.0 ms baseline; can I put that number in my status report?
evals.expected_output: The CSV has 96 evaluations across 6 generations; 17 rows have the invalid score "*" and must be excluded (coerce score_1 to numeric, as in the skill's top-K snippet), leaving 79 valid rows. Top 5 by lowest score_1: 0.9167 (generation 5, params 297da195...), 0.9168 (generation 4, params 0f5cbe40...), 0.9173 (generation 5, params 78237d6c...), 0.9186 (generation 3, params 2cd1048f...), 0.9232 (generation 4, params 253b8983...). The ~8% figure should not go in the report: search-time scores use only 5-15 trials per evaluation and a shared cache, and the best of many evaluations will look good partly by chance (the multiple-comparisons false-positive pattern). Re-measure the no-ACF baseline and each top-K candidate at validation settings (at least 50 warmup and 100 trials, fresh cache, locked GPU clocks), then apply the ship rule: Welch's t-test p < 0.05, Cohen's d > 0.2 (preferably > 0.5), and candidate mean below baseline mean.
assertions: Excluded the 17 invalid "*" score rows by converting score_1 to numeric before ranking
Listed the five lowest score_1 values (0.9167, 0.9168, 0.9173, 0.9186, 0.9232) with their generation and params
Advised against reporting the search-time ~8% as a speedup because the best of many noisy evaluations can be a multiple-comparisons false positive
Recommended re-measuring the baseline and the top-K candidates with at least 100 trials and 50 warmup runs on a fresh cache before claiming anything

evals.prompt: I re-measured the winning CompileIQ ACF for our GEMM kernel against the no-ACF baseline: 100 trials each, fresh cache, GPU clocks locked. The per-trial latencies in ms are in /workspace/input/samples_gemm_candidate.csv (columns baseline_ms and candidate_ms). Is the speedup real, and is it OK to ship this ACF?
evals.expected_output: Yes, it passes the gate. Baseline mean 1.0010 ms (std 0.0116), candidate mean 0.9614 ms (std 0.0106): mean speedup about 1.041x (median speedup also about 1.04x). Welch's t-test p is about 2e-63 and Cohen's d is about 3.56, so p < 0.05, d > 0.2 (and above the preferred 0.5), and the candidate mean is lower, so validate_speedup reports significant=True. Neither rejection check fires: the candidate mean is lower (not lucky-min), and the p5-p95 range is 0.0362 ms versus 0.0358 ms for the baseline, about 1% wider, well under the 25% higher-variance threshold. Decision KEPT: save the ACF as best.acf and record the result in validation-log.csv.
assertions: Ran validate_speedup from welch_validate.py on the two columns, or computed an equivalent Welch's t-test plus Cohen's d
Reported a mean speedup of about 1.04x (baseline about 1.001 ms, candidate about 0.961 ms)
Reported p well below 0.05 and Cohen's d about 3.6, satisfying the ship rule
Checked the lucky-min and higher-variance patterns and found that neither applies
Concluded the candidate can be kept and shipped as best.acf, with the result logged

evals.prompt: CompileIQ found an ACF for our attention kernel. I benchmarked it 100 times alongside the baseline; the data is in /workspace/input/samples_attention_candidate.csv (columns baseline_ms and candidate_ms). The fastest run dropped from 0.9732 ms to 0.9321 ms, so about 4.4% faster. I'm about to announce that to the team. Sanity-check me first?
evals.expected_output: Do not announce it; this is the lucky-min false positive. The minimums do drop (0.9732 to 0.9321 ms), but the means do not: baseline mean 0.9994 ms, candidate mean 1.0029 ms, so the candidate is slightly slower on average (mean speedup about 0.9965x; medians 1.0000 vs 1.0069 ms). Welch's t-test p is about 0.126 and Cohen's d is about -0.22, so validate_speedup reports significant=False. reject_lucky_min fires because the optimized mean is not lower than the baseline mean, and reject_higher_variance also fires: the candidate's p5-p95 range is 0.0881 ms versus 0.0376 ms, about 135% wider, far above the 25% threshold. Decision: REJECTED. Compare means, not minimums.
assertions: Ran validate_speedup from welch_validate.py, or computed an equivalent Welch's t-test plus Cohen's d
Compared means rather than minimums and reported that the candidate mean (about 1.003 ms) is not below the baseline mean (about 0.999 ms)
Identified the lucky-min false-positive pattern
Reported that the result is not significant (p about 0.13, Cohen's d negative)
Told the user not to announce the 4.4% speedup; the candidate is rejected

evals.prompt: Validation run for a CompileIQ softmax ACF: 100 baseline trials and 100 candidate trials, latencies in ms, in /workspace/input/samples_softmax_candidate.csv (columns baseline_ms and candidate_ms). I ran a t-test myself and got p < 0.05, so I think it's good to ship. Can you confirm with the proper checks before I do?
evals.expected_output: Do not ship. The statistical gate alone passes: Welch's t-test p is about 0.017, Cohen's d is about 0.34 (above 0.2 but below the preferred 0.5), and the candidate mean 0.9956 ms is below the baseline mean 1.0002 ms, a mean speedup of only about 1.0047x (0.5%). But the higher-variance check fails: the candidate's p5-p95 range is 0.0553 ms versus 0.0305 ms for the baseline, about 81.5% wider, far above the 25% threshold (candidate std 0.0173 vs 0.0088 ms). Per the skill's higher-variance pattern the ACF mostly spread the distribution rather than speeding anything up, so the decision is REJECTED:higher_variance.
assertions: Ran validate_speedup and reject_higher_variance from welch_validate.py, or computed equivalent statistics including the p5-p95 ranges
Reported p about 0.017 and Cohen's d about 0.34, with a mean speedup of only about 0.5%
Reported that the candidate p5-p95 range is about 81% wider than the baseline, above the 25% threshold
Identified the higher-variance false-positive pattern and rejected the candidate despite p < 0.05

evals.prompt:
My CompileIQ search just finished. The best config scored 3.5% faster than baseline, measured with 10 trials per evaluation and CIQ_KEEP_CACHE=1 on during the search. To save time I was going to reuse those search-time samples for the significance test, and for the re-check run:

    --opt-cmd "PTXAS_OPTIONS='--apply-controls=best.acf' python bench.py 2>&1 | grep mean"

Anything wrong with this plan?
evals.expected_output: Three problems. (1) Do not reuse search-time samples: validation N is independent of optimization N, and the search-time numbers (5-15 trials, shared cache) are too noisy to ship from. Re-measure both the no-ACF baseline and the candidate with at least 50 warmup runs and at least 100 trials, with GPU clocks locked. (2) Because CIQ_KEEP_CACHE=1 was on during the search, validation must wipe ~/.cache/compileiq or use a fresh TRITON_CACHE_DIR and HELION_SKIP_CACHE=1; otherwise the optimization-time numbers reappear and nothing is being validated. (3) welch_validate.py runs commands without a shell: the leading PTXAS_OPTIONS=... assignment is fine (it becomes an environment override), but the pipe and 2>&1 redirection are not supported. Drop them, since the default --score-regex 'mean: ([0-9.]+)' already extracts the score from stdout, or wrap the pipeline in a script and pass the script. Then apply the ship rule: p < 0.05, Cohen's d > 0.2, and candidate mean below baseline mean.
assertions: Told the user not to reuse search-time samples and to re-measure baseline and candidate with at least 100 trials and 50 warmup runs
Said the cache from the CIQ_KEEP_CACHE=1 search must be wiped (~/.cache/compileiq) or bypassed with a fresh TRITON_CACHE_DIR / HELION_SKIP_CACHE=1
Explained that the helper runs commands without a shell, so the pipe and redirection will not work, while the leading PTXAS_OPTIONS= assignment is supported
Suggested dropping the pipe in favor of --score-regex, or wrapping the pipeline in a script
